overview: Evergy is a public utility holding company headquartered in Kansas City, Missouri, formed in 2018 from the merger of Westar Energy and Great Plains Energy (parent of Kansas City Power & Light). Evergy operates integrated, rate-regulated electric utilities -- primarily Evergy Kansas Central and Evergy Metro, plus Evergy Missouri West -- that generate, transmit, distribute and sell electricity to approximately 1.7 million residential, commercial and industrial customers across Kansas and Missouri. The company holds roughly 15,800 MW of owned generating capacity and renewable power purchase agreements across coal, natural gas, nuclear (94% indirect interest in Wolf Creek) and a growing wind/solar/storage fleet, and reports as a single operating segment on the Nasdaq under the symbol EVRG.

business_model.summary: Evergy earns a regulated return on and of capital invested in its electric generation, transmission and distribution rate base, as set by the Kansas Corporation Commission (KCC), the Missouri Public Service Commission (MPSC) and, for transmission, FERC. Revenue is almost entirely cost-of-service/rate-base driven, making it highly recurring and non-discretionary (essential electric service to a captive franchise customer base), with earnings growth tied to rate base expansion, allowed ROEs, retail sales growth and a rapidly emerging large-load/data-center customer class rather than price or volume competition.
business_model.customer_type: Regulated franchise service to approximately 1.5 million residences, 0.2 million commercial firms and 7,400 industrial/municipal/other-utility customers, plus an emerging large-load/data-center industrial class served under new Large Load Power Service (LLPS) tariffs
business_model.geographic_mix: Kansas and Missouri only; Evergy expects 2026 Kansas and Missouri jurisdictional retail revenues of approximately 60% and 40%, respectively. Evergy Kansas Central serves ~751,000 customers in central/eastern Kansas; Evergy Metro serves ~591,800 customers in western Missouri and eastern Kansas (~55%/45% MO/KS split); Evergy Missouri West serves Missouri customers. FY2025 operating revenues were $5,961.6 million.

competitive_position.market_position: Sole regulated electric utility within its exclusive Kansas and Missouri franchise territories under the fully integrated regulated retail utility model -- Evergy does not compete to supply or deliver electricity to retail customers in its service area, though both states retain the legislative option to authorize retail choice. Evergy competes with other regional utilities and independent power producers to attract large-load/data-center customers and competes in the SPP Integrated Marketplace to sell surplus wholesale power.

moat_factors.description: Exclusive legal right to serve native-load retail customers across Kansas and Missouri; Missouri and Kansas both operate on the fully integrated/regulated model with no retail choice, so new entrants cannot duplicate wires infrastructure

Allowed to earn a regulator-approved return on and of invested capital; fuel and purchased power cost pass-throughs (FAC/property tax trackers) and Kansas/Missouri PISA provisions (deferring 85-90% of depreciation and return between rate cases) reduce volume and regulatory-lag risk

KCC- and MPSC-approved LLPS rate plans require data center/large-load customers (>75 MW) to post two years of minimum-bill collateral, pay a minimum bill set at 80% of contracted demand, and sign 12-year contracts (plus up to 5 years of transitional load), which de-risks the large-load growth pipeline for existing ratepayers and shareholders alike

Investment-grade ratings (S&P BBB+ at the holding company, up to A at the secured-debt operating subsidiaries) and an uncapped shelf registration support continued large-scale capital market access, though credit metrics are stretched by a rapidly growing capital program

weaknesses: No pricing power or ability to grow outside the rate-base/allowed-ROE framework set by the KCC, MPSC and FERC -- all growth must be approved by regulators

Geographic concentration -- Evergy operates almost exclusively in Kansas and Missouri, with no diversification into other states or unregulated businesses, increasing exposure to local economic, legislative and weather factors

Legacy coal generation still approximately 37% of total capacity (Jeffrey Energy Center, La Cygne, Iatan, Hawthorn, Lawrence), exposing Evergy to environmental compliance costs, CCR rule risk and stranded-asset/securitization risk as the fleet modernizes

Heavy and growing reliance on debt and equity capital markets ($12.3 billion of planned debt issuance and $3.3 billion of equity issuance 2026-2030) to fund an enlarged capital plan, which dilutes per-share growth and raises financing-cost sensitivity

Large-load/data-center pipeline, while substantial (~2.6-3.1 GW of signed agreements plus a targeted 5-7 GW ultimate ambition), remains partly unexecuted; actual load materialization, timing and permitting/infrastructure build-out could fall short of plan

growth_drivers: Rate base growth from a $21.6 billion five-year (2026-2030) capital investment plan -- up from $25.2-27.4 billion (2025-2029 figure cited previously) and roughly 24% larger than the prior plan -- driving a projected rate base CAGR of approximately 12% (rate base expected to grow from roughly $20.7 billion in 2025 toward ~$36 billion by 2030)

Large-load/data-center demand: Evergy has signed electric service agreements for approximately 2.6-3.1 GW of projected peak steady-state load (including a 710 MW Google Kansas City data center and expansions for Panasonic and other large customers), with management targeting 5-7 GW of ultimate large-load agreements and retail demand growth of roughly 7-8% annually through 2030

New combined-cycle and simple-cycle natural gas generation -- approximately $9.3 billion of new generation capex through 2030, including two ~705 MW CCGT plants in Kansas (Sumner and Reno counties, online spring 2029/2030) and a 440 MW simple-cycle plant in Missouri (2030) -- plus renewable additions (Kansas Sky solar, Sunflower Sky, Foxtrot) and exploration of battery storage and nuclear

Constructive new regulatory mechanisms: Missouri's SB4 (construction-work-in-progress in rate base for new gas generation, PISA extension through 2035) and the KCC/MPSC-approved LLPS large-load tariffs reduce regulatory lag and shift large-load-driven infrastructure cost risk away from existing ratepayers

Long-term adjusted EPS growth guidance of 6-8%+ annually through 2030 (off the original FY2026 adjusted EPS midpoint of $4.24), with management guiding to EPS growth exceeding 8% annually from 2028 through 2030 as the capital plan ramps

Transmission growth via Evergy's FERC-regulated transmission formula rate and its equity-method stakes in Transource Energy (13.5%) and Prairie Wind Transmission (50%), both benefiting from regional (SPP) transmission expansion

business.description: Capital and EPS plans increasingly depend on data center and large-load customers (currently ~2.6-3.1 GW signed against a 5-7 GW ambition); delay, scale-back or cancellation of these projects could leave the capital program overbuilt relative to realized demand

Nearly all revenue is earned under KCC, MPSC and FERC frameworks within just two states; adverse rulings in either jurisdiction materially affect consolidated results, and the Evergy Companies note this concentration increases exposure to local/regional factors

business.risk: Execution risk on a rapidly scaling and more complex capital program
business.description: Construction of new CCGT and simple-cycle gas plants, solar facilities and transmission projects carries cost-overrun, single-vendor (power island equipment), labor, tariff and supply-chain risk; the Kansas Sky solar project has already been delayed by litigation over local permitting

business.risk: Coal and legacy generation transition / stranded-asset risk
business.description: Coal remains ~37% of owned capacity; eventual retirement or conversion of units (Jeffrey Energy Center, La Cygne, Iatan, Hawthorn, Lawrence) outside IRP-contemplated timing risks disallowed cost recovery, and some insurers are limiting coverage for coal-exposed utilities

financial.description: Long-term debt rose to roughly $15.0 billion at Evergy consolidated (Sept 2026) from $13.4 billion at year-end 2025; the company plans to issue ~$12.3 billion of debt and ~$3.3 billion of equity 2026-2030, raising interest expense (up ~$53 million in 2025 and ~$50 million YTD Sept-2026) and sensitivity to capital-market conditions

Evergy is actively issuing shares via forward sale agreements and ATM programs (3.9 million new shares issued in September 2026 alone, raising ~$321 million) and still has ~$1.4 billion of convertible notes outstanding (partially repurchased in 2026) that dilute EPS as conversion thresholds are crossed

financial.risk: Capital structure covenants limit financial flexibility
financial.description: Evergy and its subsidiaries are bound by minimum common-equity ratios (35-40% of capitalization) and consolidated debt/capitalization covenants (not more than 0.65:1.00) that constrain the mix of future financing and could restrict dividend payments if credit ratings fall below BBB-/Baa3

regulatory.risk: Multiple pending rate cases with uncertain outcomes
regulatory.description: Evergy Metro's February 2026 MPSC filing (~$140 million ask, 10.5% ROE) is pending an order expected by year-end 2026 with new rates in January 2027; Evergy Missouri West's November 2026 MPSC filing seeks ~$229.5 million (10.25% ROE), with new rates expected October 2027 -- outcomes and timing are not guaranteed

Kansas and Missouri PISA provisions cap the annual revenue-requirement impact from deferred plant-in-service amounts (1.5%/2.5% per year); an accelerating capital program could cause Evergy to exceed these limits, delaying cost recovery

regulatory.risk: Nuclear production tax credit treatment uncertainty
regulatory.description: IRS guidance expected in 2026 on the computation of gross receipts for nuclear PTC eligibility could significantly reduce available credits; benefits are also subject to return to customers through regulatory proceedings, including Evergy Metro's pending Missouri rate case

Evolving CCR Part A/B rules, Clean Air Act requirements and potential future GHG rules could require significant incremental capex or force earlier-than-planned coal retirements, with recovery of related costs not guaranteed

macro.description: A large, growing capital plan funded continuously with debt and equity issuance makes Evergy sensitive to higher-for-longer rates, which raise financing costs and can pressure the economics of allowed ROEs relative to the cost of capital

Evergy is a summer-peaking utility with roughly one-third of retail revenue recorded in Q3; favorable weather drove a large share of the 2026 adjusted EPS guidance raise, and management has flagged that the incremental 2026 profit is viewed internally as weather-driven rather than a permanent step-up in earnings power

Coal, uranium, and natural gas costs are largely passed through via fuel adjustment clauses in Kansas and Missouri, limiting -- but not eliminating -- margin risk from price swings or geopolitical disruption to fuel supply (e.g., non-Russian uranium sourcing)

New generation construction depends on a single vendor for gas-plant power island equipment and imported materials (steel, copper, aluminum) subject to tariffs, raising cost and schedule risk for the ~$9.3 billion new-generation capital program

macro_factors.industry_outlook: US regulated electric utilities are in a historically strong investment cycle driven by grid modernization, electrification and especially data center/AI-driven load growth; Evergy is among the most levered Midwest names to this theme given its approved large-load tariffs and signed hyperscaler-related agreements (including Google) in the Kansas City corridor
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low -- regulated utility earnings are largely non-cyclical and defensive, insulated from broad economic cycles by rate-base economics and fuel cost pass-throughs, though the emerging large-load/data-center demand stream introduces a newer, less-tested growth variable with its own execution risk
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High -- a large and growing capital program funded with continuous debt and equity issuance means financing costs and cost of capital directly affect earnings growth and credit metrics
key_input_costs: Materials/equipment for gas and renewable buildout (steel, copper, aluminum, turbines, battery storage, solar components)

recent_developments.event: Evergy reported Q3 2026 adjusted EPS of $2.58 (vs. $2.03 prior year, beating consensus by ~12%) on favorable weather and higher weather-normalized demand; raised full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $4.35-$4.50 from $4.14-$4.34 while reaffirming the 6-8%+ long-term EPS growth target through 2030 off the original $4.24 midpoint
Evergy Missouri West filed a rate case with the MPSC seeking an approximately $229.5 million annual revenue increase (10.25% ROE, 52% equity), with new rates expected effective October 2027

Evergy signed and amended additional electric service agreements with large-load/data-center customers (including a 710 MW Google Kansas City data center and expansions for Panasonic and other customers), bringing signed large-load agreements to roughly 2.6-3.1 GW of projected peak steady-state demand, with management targeting an eventual 5-7 GW pipeline

Evergy Metro filed a Missouri rate case seeking a ~$140 million annual increase (10.5% ROE); an evidentiary hearing occurred in October 2026 with partial stipulations reached and an MPSC order expected before year-end 2026, new rates effective January 2027
Evergy repurchased $244.1 million of its $1.4 billion 4.50% Convertible Notes for ~$308.6 million, leaving $1,155.9 million outstanding

KCC and MPSC approved new Large Load Power Service (LLPS) rate plans establishing a tariff framework (minimum billing at 80% of contracted demand, two-year collateral requirement, 12-year minimum term) for large load customers above 75 MW, protecting existing customers from data-center-driven cost increases
KCC approved Evergy Kansas Central's unanimous rate case settlement ($128.0 million annual increase); new rates took effect October 2025
Missouri Senate Bill 4 (SB4) signed into law, enabling construction-work-in-progress (CWIP) in rate base for new gas-fired generation and extending Missouri's PISA provisions through 2035

items.notes: Raised from original guidance of $4.14-$4.34, driven by favorable weather and higher weather-normalized retail demand (including new data center load); FY2025 adjusted EPS was $3.83 and GAAP diluted EPS was $3.66

Management guides to EPS growth exceeding 8% annually from 2028 through 2030 as the capital plan ramps; the ~250 basis point gap versus rate base growth is described by management as a steady historical relationship
Up roughly 24% from the prior plan; includes ~$9.3 billion of new generation (primarily natural gas, renewables and battery storage) to serve historic economic development and large-load demand

Up from an earlier ~11.5% estimate (rate base guided from ~$20.7 billion in 2025 toward ~$36 billion by 2030), reflecting the larger capital program and large-load-driven generation/transmission investment
Up from a prior ~6% forecast, driven by data center and large-load customer additions
Includes refinancing of $3.9 billion of long-term debt maturities and open-market repurchases, subject to market conditions
To be executed via ATM program forward sale agreements, subject to market conditions
Quarterly dividend raised 4% to $0.7225 per share in 2026 (from $0.6950); Evergy targets continued annual dividend growth within this payout range

guidance.management_commentary: Management frames the 2026 adjusted EPS beat as substantially weather-driven and is holding the long-term 6-8%+ EPS growth algorithm to the original $4.24 2026 midpoint rather than rebasing higher off the raised guidance, signaling that near-term outperformance is not viewed as a permanent step-up in earnings power. Management continues to emphasize the large-load/data-center pipeline (currently ~2.6-3.1 GW signed, targeting 5-7 GW) as the key swing factor for the capital plan and rate base growth, while highlighting the LLPS tariff protections and Missouri SB4/PISA mechanisms as reducing regulatory lag and ring-fencing existing customers from large-load-driven cost increases. Pending Missouri rate cases (Evergy Metro and Evergy Missouri West) and continued reliance on debt/equity markets to fund the enlarged capital program remain the principal flagged execution risks.

bull_case: Among the most levered Midwest regulated utilities to the data center/AI-driven demand theme, with signed large-load agreements (~2.6-3.1 GW, including a 710 MW Google data center) against a targeted 5-7 GW pipeline, supporting 7-8% annual retail demand growth and ~12% rate base CAGR through 2030

Newly approved LLPS large-load tariffs (minimum billing at 80% of contracted demand, two-year collateral, 12-year minimum terms) structurally protect existing ratepayers and shareholders from large-load execution risk, a more de-risked structure than some peers
Constructive regulatory environment: Missouri's SB4 (CWIP in rate base for new gas plants) and extended PISA provisions in both states reduce regulatory lag versus the historical utility model

Diversified, largely de-risked cash flows: substantially all revenue is rate-regulated with fuel-cost and property-tax pass-through mechanisms that limit (though do not eliminate) commodity and tax-rate risk

Double-digit long-term EPS growth trajectory (6-8%+ through 2030, exceeding 8% in 2028-2030) is above the typical regulated utility peer range of 5-7%, with Q3 2026 results beating consensus by over 12%
bear_case: Large-load/data-center demand remains only partially contracted (2.6-3.1 GW signed vs. a 5-7 GW ambition); any delay, scale-back or cancellation of hyperscaler projects could leave the enlarged $21.6 billion capital plan overbuilt relative to realized revenue

Heavy and continuing reliance on new debt (~$12.3 billion) and equity (~$3.3 billion) issuance through 2030 dilutes per-share growth and signals the balance sheet cannot fund the capital plan from internal cash flow alone; convertible note dilution is already measurably reducing EPS

Management's choice to hold the long-term EPS growth algorithm to the original (lower) 2026 midpoint, despite a weather-driven guidance raise, suggests the incremental 2026 upside may not be durable or repeatable

Multiple simultaneous and unresolved Missouri rate cases (Evergy Metro ~$140 million ask, Evergy Missouri West ~$229.5 million ask) create binary regulatory outcomes that could compress allowed returns versus plan assumptions

Legacy coal generation (~37% of capacity) and two-state (Kansas/Missouri) geographic concentration leave Evergy exposed to environmental compliance costs, stranded-asset risk, and idiosyncratic regional/legislative developments with no diversification cushion available to larger multi-state peers
